newsitem.title: USA: Clinton plays up education in Ohio visit.
newsitem.headline: Clinton plays up education in Ohio visit.

text.p: With just two weeks of campaigning left before voters elect a leader, President Bill Clinton played it safe on Monday and let his surrogates duel with the Republicans in a campaign financing controversy.

Clinton, at a rain-soaked rally at Cuyahoga Community College, dwelt on an issue that has helped propel him into a double-digit lead over Republican Bob Dole in pre-Nov. 5 election polls -- improving access to higher education. His specific focus was direct student loans, an initiative that he steered through Congress in 1993.

"It made it quicker and cheaper for young people to get college loans. Sixteen hundred schools now participate in that programme, including Cuyahoga Community College and 69 others in Ohio," Clinton said. "Ten million Americans have saved an average of $190 each on their college loans, and even more important, it means you can borrow money for college without worrying how you're going to pay it back."
Clinton, referring to Dole only as "my opponent," said the challenger had opposed authorising student loans 31 years ago and fought the direct programme three years ago.

He ignored Dole's election end-game call for sweeping changes in how U.S. campaigns are financed. But Clinton campaign spokesman Joe Lockhart noted that the former senator had not pushed the issue during his 35 years in Congress.

"It's curious that a career politician who may be two weeks from ending his career now embraces campaign finance reform," Lockhart said. He added that Dole's stance was "like (suicide doctor) Jack Kevorkian giving a lecture on the sanctity of life."

Dole, who was campaigning in Michigan on Monday, issued the reform call on Sunday in an effort to exploit a potential liability for his front-running opponent -- charges that the Democratic Party took contributions from foreign fat cats.

Dole said only U.S. citizens eligible to vote should be able to give money to candidates and he also urged other reforms including a ban on "soft money" donations from corporations, labour unions and other groups to help political parties finance campaign advertisements and other activities.
Clinton surrogates said Dole was guilty of hypocrisy since he had accepted contributions from foreign donors himself.

Ohio, with 21 of the 270 electoral votes needed to capture the White House and a long history of backing winners in presidential races, is a battleground state in Clinton's contest with Dole. The latest tracking poll in the bellwether state showed Clinton ahead of Dole by 14 percentage points.
Clinton also planned to campaign in Michigan on Monday, but his only public event there was a groundbreaking ceremony for an extension to the Detroit metropolitan airport.
